lessons.title: Segment Tree On Problems
lessons.objective: Apply segment trees to problems beyond array range queries by recognising when a problem's state can be encoded in segment tree nodes with an associative merge operation.
concepts: Segment tree generalisation: any problem with associative merge on ranges
Count of Range Sum (#327): segment tree on coordinate-compressed prefix sums
Falling Squares (#699): segment tree with lazy propagation on coordinate-compressed x-positions
Coordinate compression: map large value range to small index range
Custom node type: nodes can store structs, not just integers
Associativity requirement: merge(a, merge(b, c)) == merge(merge(a, b), c)
Segment tree beats: push-down min/max operations for harder range queries
O(n log n) with coordinate compression for large-value problems
lessons.explanation: Segment trees generalise beyond summing arrays. The key requirement is an associative merge function. For Falling Squares (#699): squares fall onto a number line and stack. Each square lands at position [l, r] with height h; find the maximum height after each square. The x-positions can be large (up to 10^8) but there are only n squares (at most 2n distinct x-coordinates). Coordinate compress the x-coordinates to [1..2n], build a lazy segment tree on this compressed range, and for each square apply a range-max update (heights only increase when a square stacks). Query the maximum height in [l, r] after each square. Count of Range Sum (#327): given an array, count subarrays whose sum is in [lower, upper]. Using a segment tree on sorted prefix sums (or merge sort), each prefix sum query checks how many previous prefix sums are in a valid range. The merge function is 'count the number of elements' — an integer count, which is associative. Any problem where you need to: (1) query an aggregate over a range, (2) update individual or range values, and (3) the aggregate has an associative merge — is a segment tree candidate.
lessons.analogy: Applying segment trees to non-array problems is like using a universal filing system. The filing system (segment tree structure) works for any type of document (problem type) as long as you can define how two file cabinets (tree nodes) combine their contents (associative merge). Once you identify the merge operation, the filing system handles the efficient range queries and updates automatically.

code_example.explanation: Falling Squares uses range-max (not range-sum) lazy propagation. The lazy tag is the maximum height pending push-down; when a child already has a higher value, the parent's lazy tag does not reduce it. This 'max-preserving' lazy propagation is correct because heights only increase: a square landing on a higher base will produce a higher column, and we want the maximum at each position.

common_mistakes: Forgetting coordinate compression for large-value inputs — x-positions up to 10^8 cannot directly index a segment tree; compress to [1..2n] first before building the tree
Using range-add instead of range-max for Falling Squares — squares set the height to max(current, base+size), not add to current; the operation is range-max, not range-add

Not verifying associativity of the merge function before applying segment tree — if the merge is not associative, the segment tree query will give wrong results; always verify merge(merge(a,b),c) == merge(a,merge(b,c))
lessons.interview_relevance: Applying segment trees to non-array problems is a senior-level skill. Falling Squares is a hard problem that requires both coordinate compression and lazy segment tree. Interviewers use this problem to distinguish candidates who understand the segment tree as a general framework versus those who have only memorised the range sum variant.

flashcards.front: Segment tree applied to arrays of segments: typical use?
flashcards.back: When queries are over ranges and each update touches one element. Examples: range min/max with point updates, count of elements in a range satisfying a property (with coordinate compression), merging complex aggregates (max non-overlapping intervals in a range).

flashcards.front: Segment tree beats (Ji Driver Segmentation): what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Range update with complex operations: e.g., 'set all elements in [l,r] to min(arr[i], x)' or 'set arr[i] = min(arr[i], x) for all i in [l,r]'. Standard lazy propagation fails because min(arr[i], x) depends on arr[i]'s current value. Segment tree beats handles this in O(n log² n).

flashcards.front: Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n) using segment tree?
flashcards.back: Build segment tree over value range. For each element x (processed left to right): query max LIS length for values in [1, x-1]; update position x with that value+1. Uses segment tree on VALUE not INDEX. O(n log n) total.

flashcards.front: Count of range sum (#327): segment tree approach?
flashcards.back: Compute prefix sums. Count pairs (i,j) where lower ≤ prefix[j] - prefix[i] ≤ upper. Equivalent to: for each j, count prefix sums in [prefix[j]-upper, prefix[j]-lower]. Use merge sort or BIT with coordinate compression. O(n log n).

flashcards.front: Segment tree with merge of node information: when needed?
flashcards.back: When the aggregate at an internal node CANNOT be computed from the two children's aggregates alone. Example: 'longest subarray with sum ≥ k' — you need to merge left suffix with right prefix. Each node stores: total, leftMax, rightMax, leftSum, rightSum. More complex but still O(log n).

flashcards.front: Persistent segment tree: what does 'persistent' mean?
flashcards.back: Each update creates a NEW VERSION of the segment tree (sharing unchanged nodes with the previous version via path copying). Allows queries on ANY historical version. O(log n) per update (creates log n new nodes), O(log n) per query on any version, O(n log n) total space.

quiz.question: LIS using segment tree on value range: arr=[3,1,2,4]. After processing arr[0]=3 (query max LIS for values [1,2]), result is?
options: 0 (no values in [1,2] yet)
1 (value 3 gives LIS=1)
quiz.explanation: Process 3: query max LIS for values in [1,2] (values strictly less than 3). No elements processed yet → result=0. LIS ending at 3 = 0+1 = 1. Update position 3 in segment tree with value 1.

quiz.question: After processing [3,1,2,4] left-to-right with segment tree LIS, what is the LIS length ending at arr[3]=4?
quiz.explanation: Process 4: query max for values [1,3] (values < 4). After processing 3(LIS=1), 1(LIS=1), 2(LIS=2): max in [1,3] = 2. LIS ending at 4 = 2+1 = 3. Answer: 3 (e.g., [1,2,4]).

quiz.question: Persistent segment tree: updating one element creates how many new nodes?
options: O(n) — all nodes
O(log n) — only the path from root to the updated leaf
O(1) — only the leaf
O(n log n) — all historical versions
quiz.explanation: Path copying: when a node is modified, create a new version of it AND all ancestors up to the root. Path length = O(log n). All OTHER nodes (not on the path) are shared with the previous version. O(log n) new nodes per update.

quiz.question: Segment tree for 'longest subarray with all elements ≤ k': why can't each node just store the max element?
options: It can — max element comparison is sufficient
You need to also track how far the valid run extends from each end (leftLen, rightLen) and total answer within the range
You need the sorted order of elements
The max element is sufficient for range min queries not max
quiz.explanation: The longest subarray may cross the midpoint. A node covering [l,r] must store: longest valid run starting from l (leftLen), longest starting from r (rightLen), and total answer (ans). The parent combines these from its children — max alone is insufficient.

theory_mcq.question: For Falling Squares, why is COORDINATE COMPRESSION necessary before applying the segment tree?
options: Coordinate compression is only for performance; the algorithm works without it

Positions can be up to 10^8 but the number of DISTINCT RELEVANT POSITIONS is at most 2*n (each square contributes at most 2 coordinates: its left edge and right edge-1); allocating a segment tree of size 10^8 would require ~400 MB; compressing to 2*n positions reduces the tree size to O(n), making the O(n log n) approach feasible; the compressed indices preserve all relative ordering and interval containment relationships
Coordinate compression converts the problem from 2D to 1D
Segment trees only work with indices 1..n; compression enforces this
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Coordinate compression: map large value range to small index range' and 'O(n log n) with coordinate compression for large-value problems' — without compression, a segment tree on positions up to 10^8 would require O(10^8) space and time, making it infeasible; compression to 2n positions reduces this to O(n log n).

theory_mcq.question: In Falling Squares, the lazy propagation uses `Math.max` instead of addition for both tree and lazy arrays. Why?
options: Math.max is used because heights can never decrease

The UPDATE semantics differ: in a range-add lazy tree, adding delta means heights increase by a fixed amount for all elements; in Falling Squares, a square SETS all heights in its range to max(current, newHeight) — it doesn't add; when a new square of height H lands on a range, every position in that range becomes max(existing_height, H); the lazy tag represents a pending SET-TO-MAX operation; combining two pending set-to-max operations: max(max(x,a),b) = max(x, max(a,b)) — they compose by taking the max of the two values
max is used because segment trees must use associative operations
Math.max prevents negative heights from appearing in the tree
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `tree[node]=Math.max(tree[node],val)` and `lazy[node]=Math.max(lazy[node],val)` — the operation is 'set to max', not 'add delta'; two pending max-set operations combine: if lazy tag is already 10 and a new value of 8 arrives, the pending tag stays 10 (max(10,8)=10); lazy tags compose by max not by addition.

logic_mcq.question: For `fallingSquares([[1,2],[2,3],[6,1]])`, trace the first two squares and explain why the answer is [2,5,5].
options: Square 1 at [1,2): height 2; Square 2 at [2,5): base=2 (overlaps), height 2+3=5; Square 3 at [6,6]: height 0+1=1; maxH=[2,5,5] ✓
Square 1: height 2; Square 2: lands next to square 1, height 3; maxH=[2,3,3]
All three squares land independently; heights=[2,3,1]; maxH=[2,3,3]
Square 2 fully overlaps square 1 so height=2+3=5; square 3 at position 6 is isolated; maxH=[2,5,5]
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: [2,5,5]; Square 1 at [1,2], size 2: covers positions [1,2]; base=0, height=2; maxH=2; Square 2 at [2,3], size 3: covers positions [2,4]; query([2,4]) includes position 2 which has height 2; base=2, height=2+3=5; maxH=5; Square 3 at [6,6], size 1: no overlap, height=1; maxH stays 5.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson states the segment tree generalisation requires the ASSOCIATIVITY of the merge operation. For Falling Squares (max merge), verify associativity: `max(max(a,b), c) == max(a, max(b,c))`.
options: max(max(3,5),2)=max(5,2)=5; max(3,max(5,2))=max(3,5)=5 ✓ — max is associative
max is not associative; the segment tree must process left-to-right only
max(max(a,b),c) is always max(a,c) — b is irrelevant
Associativity holds only for distinct values; equal values break it
logic_mcq.explanation: max IS associative: max(max(a,b),c) = max(a,b,c) = max(a,max(b,c)) for any values; this is the fundamental reason max (and min, sum, XOR, GCD) can be stored in segment tree nodes — the order of combining sub-ranges doesn't matter; non-associative operations (like average) cannot be directly used in segment trees.

syntax_mcq.question: In the Falling Squares coordinate compression, `const compress = new Map(sorted.map((v,i) => [v, i+1]))` uses `i+1` (not `i`). Why 1-indexed compression?
options: 1-indexing is required because Map indices start at 1

1-INDEXED COMPRESSION matches the segment tree's 1-indexed convention (root=1, children=2i, 2i+1); if compressed to 0-indexed and used as segment tree range, position 0 would map to segment tree node 0 which is unused (root is at index 1); the +1 shift ensures compressed coordinates 1..2n align with the segment tree's 1-indexed range [1..n]; if 0-indexed, the segment tree calls would need adjustment throughout
i+1 prevents Map from storing key 0 which has special meaning
1-indexing provides one extra position for the sentinel element
syntax_mcq.explanation: The segment tree in the lesson initialises with range [l=1, r=n]; coordinate compression uses i+1 to produce indices 1..n matching this range; 0-indexed compression would produce 0..n-1 and would require passing l=0 to the segment tree, changing the child navigation formula; the i+1 convention aligns coordinate-compressed indices with the segment tree's natural 1-indexed structure.

lessons.title: Heavy-Light Decomposition Intro
lessons.objective: Understand Heavy-Light Decomposition conceptually: how it decomposes tree paths into O(log n) chains, and why this enables O(log^2 n) path queries using a segment tree on each chain.
concepts: HLD: decompose tree into chains where each path uses O(log n) chains
Heavy edge: edge to the child with the largest subtree size
Light edge: edge to any non-heavy child
Heavy child: the child with the largest subtree among all children
Each node has at most one heavy child
Chain: maximal path of consecutive heavy edges
Property: any root-to-leaf path crosses at most O(log n) light edges
O(log^2 n) path query: O(log n) chains * O(log n) per chain segment tree query
lessons.explanation: Heavy-Light Decomposition (HLD) is an advanced tree technique that enables efficient queries on paths in a tree. Without HLD, querying the sum or maximum along a path from node u to node v requires O(n) in the worst case. With HLD, any path is decomposed into O(log n) contiguous chains, and a segment tree on each chain enables O(log n) per chain query, giving O(log² n) total. The decomposition: for each node, designate its heaviest child (the one with the largest subtree) as its heavy child. The edge to the heavy child is the heavy edge; all others are light edges. A chain is a maximal sequence of heavy edges. Key property: any path from root to a node crosses at most O(log n) light edges. Proof: each light edge transition means the subtree at least doubles in size (since the light child is not the heaviest); a subtree can at most double log n times before reaching n. This logarithmic bound is what makes HLD work. In practice, HLD is implemented by assigning DFS visit order so that each chain's nodes have contiguous indices, enabling a segment tree indexed by DFS order to answer chain queries in O(log n).
lessons.analogy: Heavy-Light Decomposition is like a highway system for a tree. Heavy edges are highways (fast travel, direct), light edges are local roads (slower, fewer). Any journey from root to any node uses at most O(log n) local roads, with highways doing most of the work. Because highways are long and contiguous, they can be stored efficiently in a segment tree. The traveller only needs O(log n) segment tree queries (one per local road transition) to traverse any path.

code_example.explanation: The key invariant in _dfs2: nodes on the same chain have contiguous DFS positions (pos values). This is achieved by always extending the heavy child first before visiting light children. Because of this, a segment tree indexed by pos can answer queries on any contiguous chain segment in O(log n). The path query then traverses O(log n) chains, each requiring one segment tree query.

common_mistakes: Not extending the heavy child first in DFS 2 — the chain's DFS positions must be contiguous; visiting light children before the heavy child breaks the contiguity invariant

Thinking HLD gives O(log n) instead of O(log^2 n) — the O(log^2 n) comes from O(log n) chain jumps times O(log n) segment tree queries; if only counting queries (not updates), the total is O(log^2 n), not O(log n)
Confusing HLD with Euler tour — HLD assigns DFS positions so chains are contiguous; Euler tour assigns positions so subtrees are contiguous; they solve different problems
lessons.interview_relevance: HLD is a competitive programming technique that appears in senior interviews at companies like Google, especially for tree path query problems. It is not asked at most product company interviews but is expected knowledge for L6+ roles and specialised competitive programming positions. Understanding HLD conceptually (the chain decomposition and O(log² n) complexity) without full implementation is the expected depth for most senior interviews.

flashcards.front: Heavy-Light Decomposition (HLD): what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: PATH QUERIES and UPDATES on trees in O(log² n). A path from u to v can cross O(n) edges in a general tree, making naive path queries O(n). HLD decomposes the tree into O(log n) contiguous chains, allowing each chain segment to be queried with a segment tree in O(log n).

flashcards.front: HLD: heavy child definition?
flashcards.back: The heavy child of node u is the child with the LARGEST SUBTREE SIZE. All other children are 'light'. A node has at most one heavy child. The heavy path continues through heavy edges only, creating maximal paths called 'heavy chains'.

flashcards.front: HLD: key property about light edges on any root-to-leaf path?
flashcards.back: Any root-to-leaf path has AT MOST O(log n) light edges. This is because each time you cross a light edge from parent to child, the subtree size at least HALVES. So after O(log n) light edges, the subtree size reaches 1 (a leaf).

flashcards.front: HLD: how to answer a path query from u to v?
flashcards.back: While u and v are on different chains: pick the node with the deeper chain top (shallowest ancestor on its chain), query its chain from chain_top to that node, move to chain_top's parent. Repeat. When on the same chain: query the segment between u and v directly. O(log n) chain segments × O(log n) segment tree query = O(log² n).

flashcards.front: HLD: DFS ordering for segment tree?
flashcards.back: DFS that always visits the heavy child FIRST. Assigns DFS entry time (in[v]) to each node. Nodes on the same heavy chain get CONSECUTIVE DFS times. The segment tree is built on this DFS-ordered array. Query on a chain segment [chain_top, node] = query segtree on range [in[chain_top], in[node]].

flashcards.front: HLD applications?
flashcards.back: Path sum/min/max on tree edges or nodes. Path updates (add value to all nodes on a path). LCA queries (as a byproduct of the chain structure). Any problem that reduces to 'aggregate over a path in a tree'.

quiz.question: Tree: root 1 with children 2,3. Child 2 has children 4,5. Child 3 has child 6. Subtree sizes: 1→6, 2→3, 3→2, 4→1, 5→1, 6→1. Heavy child of node 2?
options: 4 or 5 (tie — equal subtree sizes)
4 (first child by convention when tied)
No heavy child (both children have equal size)
2 itself
quiz.explanation: Node 2 has children 4 and 5, both with subtree size 1. It's a tie — either can be the heavy child (implementation chooses one, often the first). In practice, ties are broken arbitrarily since the log n guarantee holds either way.

quiz.question: HLD: why do light edges cause at most O(log n) chain switches on any root-to-leaf path?
options: There are at most log n nodes on any path
Each light edge crosses from parent to a child whose subtree is strictly less than half the parent's subtree size
Heavy edges are processed in O(1)
The tree is balanced
quiz.explanation: Light edge from u to v: subtree(v) ≤ subtree(u)/2 (otherwise v would be the heavy child). Starting from root (subtree size n), each light edge halves the subtree size. After O(log n) halvings: size reaches 1. So at most O(log n) light edges = O(log n) chain switches.

quiz.question: HLD path query u-to-v: O(log² n) vs O(log n). Where does the second log come from?
options: Building the segment tree costs O(log n)
Each of the O(log n) chain segments requires an O(log n) segment tree range query
Finding the LCA costs O(log n)
The DFS ordering costs O(log n)
quiz.explanation: O(log n) chain segment switches (due to light-edge property) × O(log n) segment tree range query per chain segment = O(log² n) total. With a more sophisticated structure (like a binary lifting + sparse table), the first factor can be reduced, but O(log² n) is the standard HLD bound.

quiz.question: HLD DFS ordering visits heavy child first. Why is this required?
options: It's not required — any DFS order works
Visiting heavy child first ensures nodes on the same heavy chain receive CONSECUTIVE DFS timestamps, enabling the segment tree range query on chains
It reduces the DFS runtime
It balances the tree
quiz.explanation: If the heavy child is visited first, all nodes in the heavy chain get a contiguous block of DFS timestamps [in[chain_start], in[chain_end]]. This contiguous range can be queried directly in the segment tree. Non-heavy-first ordering breaks contiguity.

theory_mcq.question: Why does any root-to-leaf path cross at most O(log n) LIGHT EDGES?
options: Light edges are rare because most edges are heavy

Every time a path TAKES A LIGHT EDGE from parent v to child u (u is NOT the heavy child of v), the subtree size STRICTLY MORE THAN HALVES: `size[u] < size[v]/2` (because u is not the largest child, so some other child has size >= size[u], meaning size[v] >= 2*size[u]); starting from n at the root and halving at each light edge: after k light edges, the subtree size is at most n/2^k; when the subtree size reaches 1 (a leaf), k <= log2(n); therefore at most O(log n) light edges on any root-to-leaf path
Light edges are limited to O(log n) because the tree has height O(log n)
A path can only cross a light edge when changing chains, which happens O(log n) times
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Property: any root-to-leaf path crosses at most O(log n) light edges' — the key inequality: when taking a light edge to child u, size[u] <= size[parent]/2 (since u lost the heavy child competition to some sibling); this halving means light edges can only occur O(log n) times before reaching a leaf; this is why HLD achieves O(log^2 n) path queries.

theory_mcq.question: In HLD's DFS2, why are heavy children extended IN THE SAME CHAIN while light children START NEW CHAINS?
options: Heavy children are extended in-chain so they have consecutive DFS positions

CONTIGUOUS SEGMENT TREE LAYOUT: the key advantage of HLD is that all nodes on a chain get CONSECUTIVE POSITIONS in the DFS order; this means any query on a chain segment corresponds to a CONTIGUOUS RANGE in the segment tree array — queryable in O(log n); if light children were included in the chain, the consecutive positions would be broken; by separating chains at light edges, each chain maps to a clean contiguous range, enabling the segment tree to answer chain queries in O(log n)
Heavy children are extended in-chain to minimise the number of DFS calls
Light children start new chains because they are at leaf level
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `this._dfs2(this.heavy[v], h); // extend chain to heavy child` — heavy extension ensures all nodes on a chain receive consecutive pos[] values; when a path query is decomposed into O(log n) chain segments, each segment is a contiguous range in the seg tree, enabling O(log n) per chain query.

logic_mcq.question: For a star graph (one central node with n-1 leaves), what is the heavy child of the center?
options: Any one of the n-1 leaves can be designated as the heavy child

ALL LEAVES have subtree size 1; the heavy child is the one with the LARGEST subtree size; since all leaves have equal size=1, the heavy child is chosen by tie-breaking (the one processed first in the adjacency list); for a star graph with n-1 leaves: the center has heavy child = one leaf (size 1 > any other subtree consideration); the center's heavy child is just one of its n-1 equal-sized children — chosen deterministically by iteration order
Star graphs have no heavy children because all subtrees are equal size
The heavy child of the center is the leaf with the highest index
logic_mcq.explanation: In the HLD implementation, `if (this.size[u] > maxSize)` updates the heavy child when a strictly larger subtree is found; for a star graph, all leaf subtrees have size=1, so the heavy child is whichever leaf appears first in the adjacency list (tie-breaking by first encounter); this is valid — any leaf can be the heavy child when all are equal size.

logic_mcq.question: Why is HLD's path query complexity O(log²n) and NOT O(log n)?
options: O(log²n) because the tree has height log n and each level costs log n

O(log²n) = O(log n) chain jumps × O(log n) per chain query: when the path from u to v spans MULTIPLE CHAINS, each chain change requires one chain segment query on the segment tree (O(log n)); there are at most O(log n) light edge crossings (= chain changes) on any u-to-v path; total = O(log n) chains × O(log n) per seg tree query = O(log²n); an O(log n) result would require O(1) per chain query, which isn't achievable with a standard segment tree
O(log²n) because each node is visited log n times during the path traversal
O(log²n) is a loose bound; the actual complexity is O(log n)
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'O(log^2 n) path query: O(log n) chains * O(log n) per chain segment tree query' — the two multiplicative log factors come from two distinct sources: the number of chain segments visited (O(log n) light edges) and the cost per chain segment query on the underlying segment tree (O(log n)); these cannot be combined into a single O(log n) without using more advanced techniques.

syntax_mcq.question: In `pathQuery`, the line `if (this.depth[this.head[u]] < this.depth[this.head[v]]) [u,v]=[v,u]` swaps u and v. What invariant does this maintain?
options: It ensures u always has a lower index than v

It ensures U IS ON THE DEEPER CHAIN HEAD: by keeping u as the one whose chain head is deeper (further from root), we always process the deeper chain first; this guarantees progress toward the root — we always climb from the deeper chain to the shallower one; processing the shallower chain first would risk infinite loops (the shallow chain's head might be above the LCA, causing overshoot); the invariant 'deeper chain head first' ensures we always make progress by jumping to the shallower side after each chain segment
The swap ensures u < v for consistent segment tree indexing
The swap ensures both u and v are always on the same chain
syntax_mcq.explanation: The invariant ensures we always process the path segment on the deeper chain first: `u = this.parent[this.head[u]]` after processing the chain segment from head[u] to u; this jumps u UPWARD (towards the root); if u's chain head were shallower than v's chain head, climbing u would potentially overshoot past the LCA; keeping u on the deeper chain ensures each jump reduces depth correctly.

lessons.title: Euler Tour And LCA
lessons.objective: Implement Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) using binary lifting in O(n log n) preprocessing and O(log n) per query, and understand the Euler tour as an alternative for range-minimum LCA.
concepts: LCA: lowest common ancestor of nodes u and v = deepest node that is an ancestor of both
Naive LCA: O(n) per query by walking up from deeper node
Binary lifting: ancestor[v][k] = 2^k-th ancestor of v
Preprocessing: ancestor[v][0] = parent[v], ancestor[v][k] = ancestor[ancestor[v][k-1]][k-1]
O(n log n) preprocessing: n nodes * log n levels
O(log n) LCA query: equalise depths then jump in powers of 2
Euler tour LCA: reduce LCA to range minimum query on Euler tour
O(n) Euler tour + O(n log n) sparse table = O(1) LCA queries
lessons.explanation: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) finds the deepest ancestor shared by two nodes. Naive approach: walk both nodes up level by level until they meet — O(n) per query. Binary lifting achieves O(log n) per query with O(n log n) preprocessing. The idea: precompute ancestor[v][k] = the 2^k-th ancestor of v (the ancestor reached by walking up 2^k levels). Base case: ancestor[v][0] = parent[v]. Transition: ancestor[v][k] = ancestor[ancestor[v][k-1]][k-1] (the 2^k-th ancestor is the 2^(k-1)-th ancestor of the 2^(k-1)-th ancestor). LCA query: first equalise the depths of u and v by lifting the deeper one. Then jump both up using the largest power of 2 that does not yet make them equal, from k=log(n) down to 0. The final answer is their parent. Euler tour LCA: perform a DFS recording every node when first visited and when returning from a child. The LCA of u and v is the shallowest node between their first appearances in the Euler tour. A range minimum query (using sparse table for O(1)) on this tour gives O(1) LCA queries after O(n log n) preprocessing.
lessons.analogy: Binary lifting LCA is like a telephone tree: to reach 8 levels up in the hierarchy, call your 4-levels-up contact, who calls their 4-levels-up contact. By combining powers of 2, you can jump any distance in O(log n) calls. The precomputation builds the 'speed dial list' for all power-of-2 ancestors, so any jump can be computed by combining these precomputed values.

code_example.explanation: The query step 2 (jump both up until just below LCA) works by finding the highest k where both ancestors differ. After the loop, u and v are the children of the LCA. Their parent (ancestor[u][0] = ancestor[v][0]) is the LCA. If k is processed from high to low, we take the largest safe jumps first, landing both pointers just below the LCA without overshooting.

common_mistakes: Not handling the case where v is an ancestor of u (or vice versa) — after equalising depths, check if u == v before the second phase; if so, u (or v) is the LCA

Processing k from low to high in the second phase instead of high to low — processing from low to high takes small steps first, potentially stopping too early; processing from high to low takes largest safe jumps first, correctly landing just below the LCA
Off-by-one in LOG — LOG = ceil(log2(n)) is the maximum number of levels; processing from k=0 to k=LOG-1 (inclusive) covers all possible depths
lessons.interview_relevance: LCA with binary lifting appears in network reliability problems and tree query problems at Google, Uber, and companies with heavy infrastructure work. The O(log n) per query after O(n log n) preprocessing is the expected solution. LCA is a building block for problems like: distance between two nodes, path sum queries, and verifying ancestry relationships efficiently.

flashcards.front: Euler Tour for LCA: what is it?
flashcards.back: A DFS traversal that records each node EVERY TIME it is visited (on entry AND on exit from each child). For a tree with n nodes: Euler tour has 2n-1 entries. Node u appears multiple times; its FIRST appearance marks entry. The LCA of u and v is the node with MINIMUM DEPTH in the Euler tour between the first appearances of u and v.

flashcards.front: Euler Tour LCA: complexity?
flashcards.back: Build: O(n) DFS → O(n) Euler tour array. Preprocess RMQ (Range Minimum Query) on depths: O(n log n) with sparse table. LCA query: O(1) (find first occurrence of u and v, query RMQ for minimum depth between them). Total: O(n log n) build, O(1) per query.

flashcards.front: Binary Lifting for LCA: what does it precompute?
flashcards.back: up[v][k] = ancestor 2^k levels above v. Build: up[v][0] = parent[v]. up[v][k] = up[up[v][k-1]][k-1]. LCA(u,v): bring both to same depth using binary lifting, then find the deepest common ancestor by testing bits from high to low. O(n log n) precompute, O(log n) per query.

flashcards.front: LCA binary lifting: step-by-step?
flashcards.back: 1) Compute depth[] for all nodes (BFS/DFS). 2) If depth[u] < depth[v]: swap. Bring v to same depth as u by lifting v using binary lifting. 3) While u ≠ v: lift both using the highest bit k where up[u][k] ≠ up[v][k]. 4) Return parent[u] (or u if u==v after depth equalisation).

flashcards.front: Euler tour for subtree queries: what property?
flashcards.back: If DFS assigns in[v] (entry time) and out[v] (exit time), the subtree of v = all nodes with in-time in [in[v], out[v]]. This converts 'query over subtree' to 'query over range [in[v], out[v]]' — usable with BIT or segment tree.

flashcards.front: LCA to distance: formula?
flashcards.back: dist(u, v) = depth[u] + depth[v] - 2 × depth[LCA(u,v)]. Where depth[v] = distance from root to v. LCA gives the deepest common ancestor; the path u→LCA→v has this length.

quiz.question: Binary lifting precompute: up[v][k] = up[up[v][k-1]][k-1]. What is up[v][2] in terms of ancestors?
options: 2nd ancestor of v
4th (2²=4) ancestor of v
1st ancestor of v
k-th ancestor of v
quiz.explanation: up[v][k] = 2^k-th ancestor. up[v][2] = 2²=4th ancestor of v. up[v][0]=parent, up[v][1]=grandparent, up[v][2]=great-great-grandparent (4 levels up).

quiz.question: Euler tour LCA: tree is root 1 with children 2,3. Node 2 has child 4. Euler tour order?
quiz.explanation: DFS: visit 1 (record). Visit 2 (record). Visit 4 (record). Backtrack to 2 (record 2 again). Backtrack to 1 (record 1 again). Visit 3 (record). Backtrack to 1 (record 1 again). Tour: [1,2,4,2,1,3,1].

quiz.question: LCA(4, 3) using Euler tour from above [1,2,4,2,1,3,1] with depths [0,1,2,1,0,1,0]: answer?
options: 1 (root)
2 (parent of 4)
quiz.explanation: First occurrence of 4: index 2. First occurrence of 3: index 5. Tour between indices 2 and 5: [4,2,1,3]. Depths: [2,1,0,1]. Minimum depth = 0 at index 4 (node 1). LCA(4,3) = 1.

quiz.question: Subtree query: in[v]=3, out[v]=7, n=10. Which nodes are in v's subtree?
options: Exactly the nodes with DFS entry time in [3,7]
Nodes 3,4,5,6,7 (by index)
All descendants of v plus v itself
Both A and C — they are equivalent
quiz.explanation: Both A and C are equivalent. DFS entry times in [in[v], out[v]] = [3,7] correspond to exactly v and all its descendants. This is the Euler tour / DFS in-out time property that enables subtree queries via range queries.

theory_mcq.question: In the Binary Lifting preprocessing, `ancestor[v][k] = ancestor[ancestor[v][k-1]][k-1]` doubles the jump distance at each level. Why does this correctly compute the 2^k-th ancestor?
options: The formula is an approximation; exact ancestors require O(n) computation

2^k = 2^(k-1) + 2^(k-1): to reach the 2^k-th ancestor, first jump 2^(k-1) steps (from v to ancestor[v][k-1]), then jump another 2^(k-1) steps from there (to ancestor[ancestor[v][k-1]][k-1]); this telescoping identity is the core of binary lifting — each level's table is computed from the previous level in O(1) per entry; the total preprocessing is O(n log n) since each of the n nodes has log n entries, each computed O(1)
The formula works only for nodes at depths that are powers of 2
ancestor[v][k] stores the k-th ancestor, not 2^k-th
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'ancestor[v][k] = ancestor[ancestor[v][k-1]][k-1]' and '2^k = 2 * 2^(k-1): jump 2^(k-1) twice' — the doubling formula correctly builds a jump table where each level k represents jumping 2^k steps; this enables O(log n) LCA queries by decomposing the depth difference into binary representation and applying the appropriate jumps.

theory_mcq.question: In the LCA query, after equalising depths, the algorithm jumps both nodes UP SIMULTANEOUSLY from high to low power-of-2. Why must it jump from HIGHEST to LOWEST (LOG-1 down to 0)?
options: Jumping from lowest to highest also works; the direction is arbitrary

GREEDY BINARY DECOMPOSITION from largest to smallest: we want to find the DEEPEST ancestors that are STILL DIFFERENT; jumping from the largest bit first ensures we take the largest possible steps while both ancestors remain distinct; if we jumped from bit 0 upward, we'd overshoot past the LCA early, potentially making both ancestors equal when they shouldn't be; descending from LOG-1 to 0 greedily 'narrows in' on the LCA from above without overshooting
Descending direction is needed for cache efficiency in the ancestor array
Jumping from lowest to highest would cause index out-of-bounds errors
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's LCA query code: `for(let k=this.LOG-1; k>=0; k--)` — the greedy approach: process bits from largest to smallest; at each step, check if jumping 2^k steps would make both equal (if so, we've overshot — don't jump); if they're still different after the jump, take it; this finds the maximum depth where u and v are still different, placing both just below the LCA; their common parent is the LCA.

logic_mcq.question: For the tree with edges [[1],[0,2,5],[1,3],[2,4],[3],[1]], `lca(3,5)=1`. Trace the LCA query.
options: Depths: 0→0, 1→1, 2→2, 3→3, 4→4, 5→2; lca(3,5): depth[3]=3>depth[5]=2; equalise: diff=1, jump 3 up by 2^0=1 → node 2; depth[2]=depth[5]=2; u=2≠v=5; jump both: 2^k ancestors differ→jump; ancestors[2][0]=1, ancestors[5][0]=1 → same! So don't jump at k=0; return ancestor[2][0]=1 ✓
lca(3,5)=2 because node 2 is at depth 2 above node 3
lca(3,5)=0 because the root is the only common ancestor
lca(3,5)=3 because node 3 is deeper
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: lca(3,5)=1; the tree is a path 0-1-2-3-4 with an additional edge 1-5; depths: 0=0,1=1,2=2,3=3,4=4,5=2; lca(3,5): depth[3]=3>depth[5]=2; diff=1 → jump u=3 by 2^0=1 → u=2; now depth[2]=depth[5]=2 but u≠v; jump both at k=LOG-1 down: ancestors[2][0]=1=ancestors[5][0]=1 → same, don't jump; return ancestor[2][0]=1.

logic_mcq.question: The Euler Tour LCA approach reduces LCA to range minimum. How many entries does the Euler tour array have for a tree with n nodes?
options: 2n-1 entries: each of the n nodes is entered once and exited once (except root exited at the end), producing 2n-1 total entries in the traversal
n entries: one per node
n log n entries: the Euler tour stores ancestors at each level
n^2 entries: all pairs of nodes
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'O(n) Euler tour + O(n log n) sparse table = O(1) LCA queries' — the Euler tour visits each edge twice (once going down, once going back up) and visits each node once per edge incident; total entries = 2n-1 for a tree with n nodes and n-1 edges; the LCA of u and v is the minimum-depth node in the Euler tour between the first occurrences of u and v.

syntax_mcq.question: The LCA uses `Math.ceil(Math.log2(n)) + 1` for LOG. Why the `+1`?
options: +1 is a safety margin; Math.ceil(Math.log2(n)) is exact

For n=1: `Math.log2(1)=0`, `Math.ceil(0)=0`, so LOG=0 would give 0 levels — the ancestor table would have 0 columns and `ancestor[v][0]=parent` could not be stored; the +1 ensures at least 1 level exists; for n=2: `Math.ceil(Math.log2(2))=1+1=2` levels — ancestor[v][0]=direct parent, ancestor[v][1]=grandparent; more generally, +1 provides a safety margin ensuring we have enough levels for the maximum possible depth, preventing off-by-one errors in queries
+1 converts 0-indexed LOG to 1-indexed
+1 handles the case where the tree is a path (worst case depth = n-1)
syntax_mcq.explanation: The +1 ensures the LOG value is always sufficient: for a chain of n nodes, the maximum depth is n-1; ceil(log2(n)) levels might be exactly enough but the +1 provides a safety margin; for n=1, ceil(log2(1))=0 without +1 would give 0 levels (broken); +1 also guards against floating-point imprecision in Math.log2 for exact powers of 2.

lessons.title: AVL Tree And Red-Black Tree Theory
lessons.objective: Explain the self-balancing invariants of AVL trees and Red-Black trees, the rotations that restore balance, and why they guarantee O(log n) height without memorising full implementation details.
concepts: Balance factor: height(left) - height(right), must be in {-1, 0, 1} for AVL
AVL rotations: single left, single right, left-right, right-left (double rotations)
Red-Black invariants: root black, no consecutive red nodes, equal black-height on all paths
Red-Black rotations + recolouring: restore invariants after insert/delete
O(log n) height guarantee: both trees maintain height <= 2*log(n)
AVL stricter: more rotations but better balance (height <= 1.44*log(n))
Red-Black more permissive: fewer rotations, used in most standard libraries
Java TreeMap, C++ std::map, Linux kernel scheduler all use Red-Black trees
lessons.explanation: Self-balancing BSTs maintain O(log n) height by rebalancing after every insert and delete. AVL trees maintain a strict balance factor: every node's left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1. When an insert violates this, one of four rotation cases restores balance: left rotation (right-heavy node), right rotation (left-heavy node), left-right rotation (left child is right-heavy), right-left rotation (right child is left-heavy). AVL trees guarantee height <= 1.44 * log₂(n). Red-Black trees maintain five invariants including the red-black colouring rules that guarantee every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes. This gives height <= 2 * log₂(n). Red-Black trees require fewer rotations per insert/delete (at most 3 rotations) compared to AVL trees (O(log n) in the worst case), which is why most standard library ordered maps use Red-Black trees. Neither tree is required to implement from scratch in most interviews, but understanding their invariants and height bounds is expected.
lessons.analogy: AVL and Red-Black trees are like two different traffic management systems for a city. AVL (stricter) ensures every intersection has the same traffic density ±1 car (balance factor ±1), requiring frequent micro-adjustments (rotations). Red-Black (more permissive) ensures the longest detour is at most twice the shortest route (height bound 2 log n), requiring fewer adjustments but allowing more variation. Both guarantee O(log n) travel time.

code_example.explanation: The four AVL rotation cases always reduce to at most two single rotations (the LEFT-RIGHT and RIGHT-LEFT cases are handled by a double rotation: one rotation to convert to the LEFT-LEFT or RIGHT-RIGHT case, then one more rotation to restore balance). After any rotation, heights must be updated from bottom to top (z first, then y in the diagrams above).

common_mistakes: Confusing when to apply left vs right rotation — left rotation is applied when the right subtree is too heavy (balance factor < -1); right rotation when the left subtree is too heavy (balance factor > 1); confusing them produces the opposite imbalance
Forgetting to update heights after rotations — heights must be updated in the correct order: the node that became a child must be updated before the node that became the parent

Thinking AVL and Red-Black trees need to be implemented from scratch in interviews — most product company interviews do not ask for full implementation; understanding invariants, rotation cases, and height bounds is sufficient
lessons.interview_relevance: AVL and Red-Black tree theory is tested in senior interviews primarily through conceptual questions: 'Why does std::map have O(log n) operations?', 'What is the balance guarantee of a Red-Black tree?', 'When would you use a self-balancing BST vs a hash map?'. Full implementation is rarely asked in product company interviews but may be asked at research-focused companies.

State three design considerations that favour Red-Black for a general-purpose sorted map.

flashcards.front: AVL tree: balance condition?
flashcards.back: For EVERY node: |height(left subtree) - height(right subtree)| ≤ 1. Self-balancing BST. After any insert or delete that violates this, rotations are applied to restore balance. Guarantees O(log n) for all operations.

flashcards.front: AVL rotations: four cases?
flashcards.back: LEFT-LEFT (LL): right rotation at the unbalanced node. RIGHT-RIGHT (RR): left rotation. LEFT-RIGHT (LR): left rotation on left child, then right rotation on parent. RIGHT-LEFT (RL): right rotation on right child, then left rotation on parent. LL and RR require 1 rotation; LR and RL require 2.

flashcards.front: Red-Black Tree: five properties?
flashcards.back: 1) Every node is RED or BLACK. 2) Root is BLACK. 3) All NIL leaves are BLACK. 4) No two consecutive RED nodes (a red node's parent and children must be black). 5) All paths from any node to its descendant NIL leaves have the SAME number of black nodes (black height).

flashcards.front: Red-Black Tree: height bound?
flashcards.back: At most 2 log₂(n+1). Because: shortest path (all black nodes) has at least log n nodes. Longest path (alternating red-black) is at most twice as long. So height ≤ 2 log n. This guarantees O(log n) for all operations despite the weaker balance condition vs AVL.

flashcards.front: AVL vs Red-Black: when is each preferred?
flashcards.back: AVL: more strictly balanced → faster LOOKUPS (fewer comparisons on average). Red-Black: fewer rotations on INSERT/DELETE → faster writes. In practice: C++ std::map uses Red-Black; database indexes often use AVL or B-Trees. For competitive programming: neither — use sorted arrays or BITs.

flashcards.front: Rotation: right rotation at node y (y's left child is x)?
flashcards.back: x becomes the new root. y becomes x's right child. x's right child (T2) becomes y's left child. Heights updated bottom-up. No node values change — only pointers rearranged. O(1) time.

quiz.question: AVL insert causes LEFT-RIGHT (LR) imbalance at node z. Fix?
options: Single right rotation at z
Left rotation at z's left child (y), then right rotation at z
Single left rotation at z
Right rotation at z's left child, then left rotation at z
quiz.explanation: LR case: imbalance at z, the taller subtree is z's LEFT child (y), and within y the taller subtree is y's RIGHT child. Fix: (1) left rotation at y (converts to LL case), (2) right rotation at z. Two rotations total.

quiz.question: Red-Black Tree: after inserting a red node, its parent is also red. What is this called and how is it fixed?
options: Black violation — convert both to black
Red violation (double red) — fix by recoloring and/or rotation depending on uncle's color
NIL violation — add sentinel
Height violation — rotate to balance
quiz.explanation: Double red violates property 4. Fix depends on uncle's color: if uncle is RED → recolor (parent and uncle → black, grandparent → red, then check grandparent). If uncle is BLACK → rotation (LL/LR/RL/RR case) + recoloring.

quiz.question: Why does Red-Black Tree guarantee O(log n) height despite NOT requiring strict height balance?
options: It doesn't — worst case is O(n)
Black-height property: all root-to-NIL paths have equal black nodes, limiting the longest path to ≤ 2× the shortest
Red nodes don't count toward height
Rotations keep the tree perfectly balanced
quiz.explanation: Black-height = k means: shortest path has k black nodes (all black, length k). Longest path has k black + k red = 2k nodes. Height ≤ 2k ≤ 2 log₂(n+1). O(log n) guaranteed.

quiz.question: For insert-heavy workloads (many inserts, few lookups), AVL or Red-Black?
options: AVL — better balance means faster lookup
Red-Black — fewer rotations per insert/delete
Identical performance
Neither — use a hash map
quiz.explanation: AVL insert can cause O(log n) rotations. Red-Black insert causes at most O(1) rotations (amortised). For insert-heavy workloads, Red-Black is preferred. For lookup-heavy (frequent searches): AVL's tighter balance means shorter path = fewer comparisons.

theory_mcq.question: An AVL tree's balance factor is `height(left) - height(right)` and must stay in {-1, 0, 1}. When is a LEFT-RIGHT rotation (not a simple right rotation) needed?
options: Left-right rotation is always needed when the tree is left-heavy

LEFT-RIGHT ROTATION is needed when: (1) the node z is LEFT-HEAVY (bf > 1) AND (2) z's LEFT CHILD y is RIGHT-HEAVY (bf(y) < 0); this 'knee' configuration cannot be fixed by a simple right rotation because rotating z right would place y as the new root with y's right subtree causing imbalance; the left-right double rotation: first rotate y LEFT (converting to left-left case), then rotate z RIGHT; example: z has left child y=5, y has right child x=7 — this right-heavy left subtree requires the double rotation
Left-right rotation is needed when the tree has more than 3 levels
Left-right rotation is always applied before right rotation for consistency
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `if(balanceFactor(node.left)<0) node.left=leftRotate(node.left); return rightRotate(node)` — the double rotation handles the 'bent' case where left child is right-heavy; a simple right rotation would not restore balance; the fix: rotate the left child left first (straightening the path), then rotate the root right.

theory_mcq.question: Red-Black trees guarantee height <= 2*log2(n+1). How is this derived from the invariants?
options: Red-Black trees have exactly log2(n) height due to perfect balance

From the invariants: (4) no consecutive red nodes means any path alternates red-black; (5) equal black-height on all paths means every path has the same number of black nodes; if the black-height is b, then any path has at least b nodes (all black) and at most 2b nodes (alternating red-black); the shortest path uses b black nodes, the longest 2b; since paths have length b to 2b, and there are n+1 leaves, b >= log2(n+1)/2; maximum height = 2b <= 2*log2(n+1); this is less strict than AVL's 1.44*log2(n) but requires fewer rotations on insert/delete
Height bound comes from the root-black requirement alone
2*log2(n+1) is an approximate bound; exact height may be higher
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Height bound: <= 2*log2(n+1)' — the bound follows from invariants 4 and 5: equal black-height b on all paths, no consecutive reds → max path length = 2b; n+1 leaves in a complete binary tree of height 2b means 2b >= log2(n+1); thus height <= 2*log2(n+1); Red-Black trades perfect balance for simpler rebalancing operations.

logic_mcq.question: For a left rotation on node z (z.right = y, y.left = T2): what is the new root and where does T2 end up?
options: New root = y; T2 becomes z's right child; z becomes y's left child — confirmed by the code
New root = z; y becomes z's left child; T2 stays as y's left
New root = T2; y and z become T2's children
New root = y; T2 becomes y's right child; z becomes y's left child
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's leftRotate code: `y.left=z; z.right=T2; return y` — y becomes the new root, z becomes y's left child, and T2 (originally y's left subtree) becomes z's right child; this preserves BST ordering: T2 has keys between z and y, so placing it as z's right maintains the invariant (z < T2 < y).

logic_mcq.question: Why do most standard libraries (Java TreeMap, C++ std::map) use Red-Black trees rather than AVL trees?
options: Red-Black trees have better worst-case performance than AVL trees

FEWER ROTATIONS ON INSERT/DELETE: AVL trees can require O(log n) ROTATIONS after an insertion (rebalancing may propagate all the way to the root); Red-Black trees require at most 2 rotations + O(log n) recolouring per insert and at most 3 rotations per delete; recolouring is much cheaper than rotation (no structural change); for map/dictionary workloads with frequent insertions, Red-Black trees have significantly smaller constant factors; AVL's slightly better search performance (shorter height) is outweighed by slower updates in insert/delete-heavy workloads
Red-Black trees are easier to implement correctly
AVL trees use more memory per node than Red-Black trees
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Red-Black more permissive: fewer rotations, used in most standard libraries' — the engineering tradeoff: AVL trees are slightly better for search-heavy workloads (shorter height); Red-Black trees are better for insert/delete-heavy workloads (constant number of rotations per modification); since map/dictionary data structures are typically used for both operations, the Red-Black tree's better mutation performance wins in practice.

syntax_mcq.question: In the AVL `balance` function, `updateHeight(node)` is called BEFORE checking the balance factor. Why must height be updated before computing bf?
options: updateHeight can be called at any time; the order doesn't affect the result

The balance factor uses `height(node.left) - height(node.right)` which reads `node.height` of children; CHILDREN'S HEIGHTS WERE ALREADY UPDATED by their own recursive balance() calls earlier in the recursion; but the CURRENT NODE's height may be stale (it stored the height before the rotation changed its subtree); updateHeight(node) recomputes `node.height = 1 + max(height(left), height(right))` using the freshly-updated children heights; if height were computed before updateHeight, it would use the old stale height giving an incorrect balance factor
updateHeight must run before balance factor to initialise the height field to a non-null value
The order only matters for leaf nodes which have no children
syntax_mcq.explanation: The recursion processes bottom-up: children are balanced first (their heights are updated), then the parent runs balance(); by the time balance(node) is called, node.left.height and node.right.height are current; updateHeight(node) recomputes node.height from these current children heights; then balanceFactor(node) correctly reads the updated height; if updateHeight were skipped or called after bf, the balance decision would be based on a stale height.

lessons.title: B-Trees And Database Index Connection
lessons.objective: Explain the B-tree structure, why it is optimised for disk-based storage, and connect it to how databases implement primary and secondary indices.
concepts: B-tree: self-balancing tree with multiple keys per node
Order m: each internal node has between ceil(m/2) and m children
All leaves at same depth: guarantees O(log_m n) height
Why B-tree for databases: minimise disk I/O (each node = one disk page)
B+ tree variant: all data at leaves, internal nodes only for routing
Primary index: built on primary key, data physically ordered
Secondary index: built on non-key attribute, stores pointers to data
Database query optimiser: uses B+ tree index for range queries, hash index for point queries
lessons.explanation: A B-tree of order m is a generalised BST where each node can hold multiple keys (up to m-1) and multiple children (up to m). All leaves are at the same depth. This design is optimised for disk-based storage: each node corresponds to one disk page (typically 4KB or 8KB). By fitting many keys per node, a B-tree of depth h can index n = m^h records. With m = 100 and h = 3, a B-tree can index 100^3 = 1 million records with only 3 disk reads. A binary search tree of the same 1 million records would require log₂(10^6) ≈ 20 disk reads — 6x more. The B+ tree variant (used in virtually all databases) stores data only at leaf nodes. Internal nodes hold only routing keys. Leaf nodes are linked in a doubly-linked list for efficient range scans. Database indices: a primary index is built on the primary key and the data is physically stored in primary key order (clustered index). A secondary index is built on a non-primary attribute and stores (attribute value, primary key) pairs; a lookup requires finding the primary key from the secondary index then using the primary index to get the actual data (two B+ tree traversals).
lessons.analogy: A B+ tree database index is like a library catalogue system with two levels. The card catalogue (internal B+ tree nodes) contains only book titles and shelf locations (routing). The actual books (data) are all on the same floor at the end (leaves). The books are physically sorted by primary key (clustering). A secondary catalogue (secondary index) sorts by author, pointing to the primary catalogue rather than directly to the books. This two-level indirection is slower but necessary when the data cannot be sorted by two keys simultaneously.

code_example.explanation: The linked leaf list in B+ trees is what makes range queries efficient. After finding the starting key via B+ tree traversal (O(log_m n) = O(log n / log m) disk reads), subsequent keys in the range are accessed by following the leaf links (O(range size / keys per node) disk reads). This makes B+ trees specifically suitable for range scans, which are common in SQL queries with BETWEEN or ORDER BY clauses.

common_mistakes: Confusing B-tree (data at all levels) with B+ tree (data only at leaves) — most databases use B+ trees because the linked leaf list enables efficient range scans; B-trees are used when point queries dominate

Thinking that a higher-order B-tree is always better — a higher m reduces disk reads but increases CPU work for searching within each node; the optimal m is determined by disk page size and key/pointer sizes
Not knowing when to choose hash index over B+ tree — hash index is O(1) for point queries but cannot support range queries; choose hash for point queries only, B+ tree for range queries or ORDER BY
lessons.interview_relevance: B-tree and database index questions appear in system design interviews at data-intensive companies (Uber, Airbnb, Stripe). The connection between algorithmic data structure choice (B+ tree vs hash) and database performance is specifically evaluated. 'Why does a database index use a B+ tree rather than a hash table?' is a classic system design interview question whose answer requires understanding range queries.

flashcards.front: B-Tree: how does it generalise a BST?
flashcards.back: A B-Tree of order m has nodes with up to m-1 keys and up to m children. Keys within a node are sorted. The subtree between key[i] and key[i+1] contains all values in (key[i], key[i+1]). All leaf nodes are at the same depth. This balances naturally even without rotations.

flashcards.front: B-Tree: minimum and maximum keys per node?
flashcards.back: All non-root nodes: at least ⌈m/2⌉-1 keys (minimum fill). At most: m-1 keys. Root: at least 1 key. The minimum fill requirement prevents the tree from degenerating. When insertion would exceed m-1 keys: split the node; when deletion would go below ⌈m/2⌉-1: merge or redistribute.

flashcards.front: B+ Tree: how does it differ from B-Tree?
flashcards.back: B+ Tree: ALL DATA is stored in LEAF nodes only. Internal nodes store only KEYS for routing. Leaf nodes are linked in a sorted doubly-linked list → efficient range scans. B-Tree: data at any node. B+ Tree is the standard for database indexes (faster range queries, fewer I/O operations for full scans).

flashcards.front: Why do databases use B-Trees (specifically B+ Trees) for indexes?
flashcards.back: 1) PAGE-ALIGNED: node size = disk page (4KB-16KB), minimizing disk I/O reads. 2) O(log_m n) height: for m=100, a tree of 10^6 records has height ≤ 3 (vs height 20 for a BST). 3) Range queries: B+ Tree leaf linked list → scan without returning to root. 4) Balanced: guaranteed O(log n) regardless of insert order.

flashcards.front: B-Tree height vs BST height for n records?
flashcards.back: BST: worst case O(n) height (sorted insert). AVL/RB: O(log₂ n) ≈ 20 for n=10^6. B-Tree order m=100: O(log₁₀₀ n) = O(log n / log 100) ≈ 20/2 = 3-4 levels for n=10^6. Each level = one disk read → B-Tree needs 3-4 reads vs AVL's 20.

flashcards.front: B-Tree: split on overflow — what happens?
flashcards.back: When a node overflows (has m keys after insert): split it into two nodes, each with ⌈m/2⌉-1 keys. The MEDIAN key is promoted to the parent. If the parent also overflows: split propagates upward. Only the root can be split into a new root → tree height grows by 1 only when root splits.

quiz.question: B-Tree of order 5 (max 4 keys per node, max 5 children): minimum keys per non-root node?
quiz.explanation: ⌈m/2⌉-1 = ⌈5/2⌉-1 = 3-1 = 2. Non-root nodes must have at least 2 keys.

quiz.question: A B+ Tree of order 100 indexing 10^6 records: maximum height?
quiz.explanation: Height ≤ 1 + log₅₀(10^6) [since minimum fill is ⌈100/2⌉=50 per non-root node] = 1 + log₅₀(10^6) ≈ 1 + 6/log₂(50) ≈ 1 + 6/5.6 ≈ 1 + 3.5 ≈ 4-5. Actually log_50(10^6) = log(10^6)/log(50) ≈ 3.6. Height ≈ 4.

quiz.question: B-Tree vs B+ Tree: for a full table scan (read all records), which is faster?
options: B-Tree — all data is at all levels
B+ Tree — leaf nodes form a linked list, scan is sequential without returning to root
Same — both O(n)
Neither — hash tables are faster for full scans
quiz.explanation: B+ Tree leaf linked list: traverse from leftmost leaf to rightmost leaf sequentially. Each disk page read gives a full node's worth of records. B-Tree: data at internal nodes too — traversal requires backtracking. B+ Tree is strictly better for sequential/range scans.

quiz.question: Why is a B-Tree's node size typically chosen to match the disk page size?
options: Coincidence
To minimise disk I/O: each node access = one disk page read. Larger nodes mean more keys per node → lower tree height → fewer disk reads per lookup
To make node splitting simpler
To match the CPU cache line size
quiz.explanation: Disk I/O is the bottleneck for database indexes. Each node access = one disk page read (4KB-16KB). A larger node holds more keys → more children → lower tree height → fewer reads per lookup. The node size is tuned to match the disk page size to avoid wasted reads.

theory_mcq.question: Why is a B-tree of order m=1000 superior to a BST for database queries on 1 million records?
options: B-trees are always better than BSTs regardless of m

DISK I/O MINIMISATION: each database access reads one DISK PAGE (typically 4-16 KB); a BST node stores one key and two pointers — each node access = one disk read = O(log2(n))=~20 disk reads for 1M records; a B-tree node of order 1000 stores up to 999 keys — one disk read reads 999 keys (one full disk page); height = log1000(1M) = log(10^6)/log(10^3) = 2 disk reads; the 10x improvement per level compounds: 2 vs 20 disk reads; disk seeks take ~5-10ms each; 2 vs 20 reads = 10x speedup × 5ms = 50ms vs 100ms per query — significant in practice
B-trees have better asymptotic complexity than BSTs
B-trees use less memory than BSTs for n records
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's comparison: 'B-tree m=1000: height=2 disk reads for 1M records' vs BST 'height~20 disk reads' — the key insight is the FANOUT: each node stores m-1 keys and m pointers; a single disk page read retrieves m child pointers, reducing tree height to log_m(n); for m=1000: log1000(10^6)=2; this directly reduces disk I/O by 10x compared to BST.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the B+ tree store ALL DATA AT LEAVES (not at internal nodes)?
options: B+ trees store data at leaves because internal nodes need to fit in a single disk page

B+ TREE LEAF SCAN ADVANTAGE: for range queries like 'SELECT * WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30', a B+ tree can traverse the leaf linked list sequentially after finding age=20; internal nodes only store routing keys (no data pointers), allowing more keys per node (higher fanout, lower height); data is only at leaves so a sequential scan reads leaves in O(records_in_range) time without backtracking; in a B-tree (data everywhere), a range query might require jumping back up and down the tree for each record in the range
B+ trees store data at leaves to simplify the deletion algorithm
Leaf storage enables O(1) point queries without traversing the tree
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'B+ tree variant: all data at leaves, internal nodes only for routing' and 'Primary index: very efficient range query (leaf scan)' — B+ leaves form a doubly linked list; once the range start is found via tree traversal, the remaining records are read by sequential leaf scanning without re-traversing the tree; this is the primary database advantage of B+ over B-trees.

logic_mcq.question: For 1 million records: BST needs ~20 disk reads but B-tree m=100 needs only 3. Verify: log100(10^6) = ?
options: log100(10^6) = 6 (using natural log)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: Math.ceil(Math.log(1e6)/Math.log(100))=3; change of base formula: log_b(x) = log(x)/log(b); log100(10^6) = log(10^6)/log(100) = 6*log(10) / (2*log(10)) = 6/2 = 3; a B-tree of order 100 for 1 million records requires at most 3 disk reads to find any record.

logic_mcq.question: A database has a range query 'SELECT * WHERE salary > 50000'. Should it use a B+ tree index or a hash index?
options: B+ TREE INDEX: hash indexes don't support range queries (unordered structure); a B+ tree locates the first record with salary>50000 in O(log n) then scans leaves sequentially for all qualifying records; hash indexes only support equality checks (WHERE salary=50000) in O(1), but for range queries, the entire hash table must be scanned — O(n)
Hash index: faster O(1) lookup per record
Both are equivalent for range queries; choose based on index size
Neither; a full table scan is always used for range queries
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Hash Index: NOT supported for range queries (unordered)' — hash functions destroy ordering information; B+ tree maintains sorted order among leaves, enabling range queries via leaf list traversal; this is why all major databases use B+ trees for range-queryable columns and hash indexes only for equality-based lookups.

syntax_mcq.question: In `BTreeNode`, the `next` pointer (`this.next = null`) creates a linked list between leaf nodes. What JavaScript pattern does this represent and why is it used?
options: next is a standard tree pointer for parent tracking

INTRUSIVE LINKED LIST: rather than maintaining a separate list data structure, the linked list connection is built INTO the node objects themselves; `node.next` points directly to the adjacent leaf node in sorted order; this enables O(1) navigation from one leaf to the next during range scans without going back up to internal nodes; it's called 'intrusive' because the list pointers are embedded in the nodes (not a wrapper structure); JavaScript linked lists are naturally implemented this way using object references
next is used for garbage collection hints in JavaScript
next stores the B-tree's sibling pointer for rebalancing
syntax_mcq.explanation: The `next` pointer in B+ tree leaf nodes creates an intrusive singly-linked list of all leaves in sorted order; this enables sequential range scans: after finding the start of a range, traverse `node.next` repeatedly to collect all qualifying records without re-traversing internal nodes; this is the key performance feature of B+ trees for range queries.

lessons.title: Advanced Tree Thinking
lessons.objective: Select the correct advanced tree technique for any tree query problem within 60 seconds, and map all Module 3 NeetCode 150 problems to their techniques.
concepts: Decision tree: array range queries vs tree path queries vs tree structure queries
Segment tree on problems: when problem state maps to associative range aggregate
LCA binary lifting: O(log n) per query after O(n log n) preprocessing
HLD: O(log^2 n) path queries on trees (conceptual awareness)
Self-balancing BST: use when O(log n) ordered insert/delete needed
B+ tree: disk-based sorted index for databases
Module 3 NeetCode 150 problems mapped
Bridge to L3-M04: advanced graph algorithms build on tree patterns
lessons.explanation: Advanced tree techniques address different query types. For array range queries (sum, min, max with updates): segment tree or Fenwick tree (Module 2). For problems where any range of an array needs custom aggregate operations: segment tree with custom node type. For tree path queries (sum or max on a path from u to v in a tree): HLD with a segment tree, O(log² n). For ancestry and path distance queries: LCA with binary lifting, O(log n) per query. For ordered dynamic set operations (insert, delete, find, floor, ceiling): self-balancing BST (AVL or Red-Black). For disk-based sorted storage with range scans: B+ tree. The module 3 problems bridge the gap between the algorithmic (segment tree, LCA) and engineering (database index, standard library ordered map) applications of advanced tree structures. A senior engineer who can trace a database range query from SQL to B+ tree leaf nodes, or explain why Java's TreeMap has O(log n) operations, demonstrates the theoretical depth that distinguishes senior from mid-level engineers.
lessons.analogy: Advanced tree thinking is the expert toolkit. A junior engineer knows basic trees (BST, binary tree). A mid-level engineer knows balanced BSTs and segment trees. A senior engineer knows when to apply HLD for tree path queries, LCA for ancestry problems, B+ trees for database indices, and sparse tables for static RMQ. Each tool is optimised for a specific operation profile; using the wrong tool is technically correct but operationally inefficient.

code_example.explanation: The Skyline Problem uses a multi-set or priority queue to track active building heights. The naive sorted array simulation is O(n²) due to indexOf and splice. The optimal solution uses a sorted multiset (like C++ multiset) for O(log n) insertions and deletions, giving O(n log n) total. In JavaScript, a Fenwick tree or segment tree on coordinate-compressed heights achieves the same O(n log n).

common_mistakes: Not recognising The Skyline Problem as a segment tree or event-based problem — the key insight is processing events (building starts and ends) in order, maintaining the current maximum height at each x-coordinate
Confusing LCA with HLD — LCA answers 'what is the deepest common ancestor of u and v?'; HLD answers 'what is the aggregate (sum/max) along the path from u to v?'; they are related but different

Thinking self-balancing BST implementation is required in interviews — in JavaScript/Python, use built-in sorted containers (sorted() in Python, or a custom balanced BST library); implementing AVL or Red-Black from scratch is rarely asked
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 3 covers 2 NeetCode 150 problems (The Skyline Problem #218 and Count of Smaller Numbers After Self #315). Both are hard-level problems that appear at Google and Meta. The complete advanced tree decision guide from this lesson enables selecting the right data structure within 60 seconds for any tree query problem encountered in a senior engineering interview.

(4) Count integers in a range [l, r] with digit sum divisible by k. (5) Support range updates and range maximum queries on an array. Map each to its Level 3 module.

flashcards.front: Advanced tree pattern recognition: 5 signals?
flashcards.back: 1) 'Query/update on PATH in a tree' → HLD + segment tree. 2) 'LCA of two nodes' → binary lifting or Euler tour + RMQ. 3) 'Subtree query' → DFS in-out time + BIT/segment tree. 4) 'Balanced BST with guaranteed O(log n)' → AVL or Red-Black. 5) 'Disk-friendly sorted structure' → B-Tree/B+ Tree.

flashcards.front: DFS in-out time encoding: three key properties?
flashcards.back: 1) SUBTREE: all nodes in subtree of v have in-times in [in[v], out[v]]. 2) ANCESTOR: u is ancestor of v iff in[u] ≤ in[v] AND out[v] ≤ out[u]. 3) HEAVY CHAIN: heavy chain nodes have consecutive in-times (if heavy child visited first in DFS). These three properties enable O(log n) tree queries via linear data structures.

flashcards.front: Why is tree DP insufficient for PATH queries but sufficient for SUBTREE queries?
flashcards.back: Subtree queries: postorder DFS naturally covers all descendants. Tree DP aggregates bottom-up → O(n) once. Path queries: a path from u to v can go UP the tree (through LCA), not just down → tree DP can't aggregate 'upward'. HLD + segment tree, or binary lifting + path decomposition, is needed for arbitrary path queries.

flashcards.front: Persistent data structures: what property do they have?
flashcards.back: All historical versions of the structure remain accessible. After each update, the previous version is unchanged. Built via PATH COPYING: only nodes on the modification path are duplicated; all other nodes are shared. O(log n) new nodes per update; O(1) per query on any version.

flashcards.front: Centroid decomposition: what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Path queries between arbitrary pairs of nodes in a tree. Find the tree's centroid (removing it splits tree into components each of size ≤ n/2). Solve all paths through the centroid, recurse on each component. Depth = O(log n). Total: O(n log n) for offline path queries.

flashcards.front: Module 3 Level 3: when would you encounter these in industry?
flashcards.back: Segment tree on problems: competitive programming, some database query engines. HLD: competitive programming, range tree data structures. LCA/binary lifting: distributed systems (lowest common ancestor in service hierarchies). AVL/RB: implemented in stdlib (std::map, Java TreeMap). B-Trees: every production database uses them.

quiz.question: Problem: 'For each query (u,v), find the XOR of all node values on the path from u to v.' Best approach?
options: BFS from u to v each query — O(n) per query
HLD + segment tree (XOR aggregate) — O(log² n) per query
DFS from root each time — O(n) per query
Precompute all pairs — O(n²) space
quiz.explanation: Path query in a tree → HLD + segment tree. XOR is associative → valid segment tree aggregate. HLD decomposes the path into O(log n) chain segments; each chain queried in O(log n) via segment tree → O(log² n) per query.

quiz.question: Is u an ancestor of v given DFS in-out times in[u]=3, out[u]=9, in[v]=5, out[v]=7?
options: No — u starts before v
Yes — in[u]=3 ≤ in[v]=5 AND out[v]=7 ≤ out[u]=9 → v is in u's subtree
Only if depth[u] < depth[v]
Cannot determine from in-out times alone
quiz.explanation: Ancestor check via in-out times: u is ancestor of v iff in[u] ≤ in[v] AND out[v] ≤ out[u]. Here: 3≤5 ✓ AND 7≤9 ✓. Yes, u is an ancestor of v.

quiz.question: Centroid decomposition: after removing the centroid of a tree with 16 nodes, each component has size at most?
quiz.explanation: Centroid property: removing the centroid splits the tree into components each of size ≤ n/2. For n=16: each component ≤ 8. This gives O(log n) = O(4) depth of recursion.

quiz.question: Persistent segment tree: query 'range sum on version k'. How many nodes does this access?
options: O(log n)
O(k log n)
O(n)
quiz.explanation: Any range query on any version accesses O(log n) nodes — same as a standard segment tree. The 'persistent' aspect only affects how updates are stored (path copying), not query complexity. O(log n) per query on any version.
